US Hazards Outlook
NWS Climate Prediction Center College Park MD
300 PM EST November 12 2026

SYNOPSIS: Mid-level low pressure is forecast to extend from the Aleutians 
southeastward to the West Coast during mid to late November. An active pattern 
is likely across the southwestern and central Contiguous U.S. (CONUS) as 
multiple low pressure systems track eastward from Nov 20-26. The enhanced 
Pacific flow favors above-normal temperatures for a majority of the CONUS. 
During week-2, portions of the Southern Plains, however, may receive their 
first freeze this season.

HAZARDS

Moderate risk of heavy precipitation for eastern portions of the Southern 
Plains and the Lower Mississippi Valley, Sat-Sun, Nov 21-22.

Slight risk of heavy precipitation for much of the eastern Plains and 
Mississippi Valley, southwestern Great Lakes region, Lower Ohio Valley, 
Tennessee Valley, Alabama, and western parts of the Southeastern CONUS, 
Fri-Sun, Nov 20-22.

Slight risk of heavy precipitation for parts of California, southwestern 
Oregon, and adjacent parts of western Nevada, Sun-Thu, Nov 22-26.

Slight risk of heavy snow for portions of the central and southern Rockies and 
adjacent parts of the central High Plains (including the Front Range area), 
Fri-Sun, Nov 20-22.

Slight risk of heavy snow for higher elevations of the Klamath and Sierra 
Nevada Mountains, 

Sun-Thu, Nov 22-26.

Slight risk of much below normal temperatures (and possible first freeze) for 
much of the Southern Plains and parts of adjacent states, Mon-Tue, Nov 23-24.

Slight risk of high winds from the Four Corners region eastward across the 
Central and Southern Rockies, most of the Plains and Mississippi Valley, 
western Great Lakes region, western Tennessee Valley, and western parts of the 
Southeastern CONUS, Fri-Mon, Nov 20-23.

Slight risk of high winds for California and southwestern Oregon, Mon-Thu, Nov 
23-26.

DETAILED SUMMARY

FOR SUNDAY NOVEMBER 15 - THURSDAY NOVEMBER 19: 
https://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/threats/threats.php

FOR FRIDAY NOVEMBER 20 - THURSDAY NOVEMBER 26: Early in week-2, a mid-level 
trough is predicted to move across the Four Corners states and into the Great 
Plains. During this time, lee cyclogenesis is forecast in the general vicinity 
of southeast Colorado, with the surface low expected to track northeastward 
towards the western or central Great Lakes region. North of the surface low, 
easterly flow is anticipated across the north-central Plains, becoming 
northeasterly over eastern portions of Wyoming and Colorado. The uncalibrated 
ECENS depicts a 20-30 percent of 6 inches or more of upslope snow over portions 
of the Central Rockies, including the more populated areas along the eastern 
foothills of the Front Range such as Denver, Fort Collins, and Cheyenne. The 
uncalibrated GEFS depicts only a 10-20 percent chance of exceeding the 6-inch 
threshold at this time, which may be a bit underdone. A slight risk of heavy 
snow is posted for western and central Colorado, extending northward into the 
Laramie Mountains of southeast Wyoming and southward into the Sangre de Cristo 
Mountains of far northern New Mexico, from Nov 20-22.



Surface high pressure moving across the northern Mid-Atlantic region will steer 
significant Atlantic and Gulf return moisture into the Central CONUS, where it 
will interact with the mid-level trough and surface cyclone. The uncalibrated 
GEFS and ECENS tools, as well as their calibrated versions (the Probabilistic 
Extremes Tools, or PETs) support a slight risk of heavy precipitation that 
encompasses much of the eastern Plains, the Mississippi Valley, and points 
eastward into the Lower Ohio Valley, and western parts of the Southeastern 
CONUS, Nov 20-22. Embedded within this widespread area is a moderate risk of 
heavy precipitation that includes the eastern Southern Plains and adjacent 
Lower Mississippi Valley, Nov 21-22. This moderate risk is supported by 50-60 
percent chances of heavy precipitation predicted by the uncalibrated ECENS, and 
at least a 20 percent chance of 3-day totals exceeding 1.5 inches and the 85th 
percentile (PET). The uncalibrated GEFS depicts a 30-40 percent chance of heavy 
precipitation within the designated moderate risk area, while the PET only 
depicts a 20 percent chance of 3-day totals exceeding 1-inch and the 85th 
percentile. Adequate Gulf moisture increases the chance for thunderstorms in 
this general region. According to the U.S. Drought Monitor valid on Nov 10, 85 
percent of Arkansas is designed with D3 to D4. This wet latter half of November 
will be largely beneficial and bring much needed drought relief to the Ozarks, 
Middle to Lower Mississippi Valley, and Southern Great Plains.



0z ECENS 10-meter wind gusts (and to a lesser extent, the PETs) favor wind 
speeds of 20 knots or greater from the Four Corners region and southern Wyoming 
eastward across most of the Plains and Mississippi Valley, the western Great 
Lakes region and into parts of the Southeast, Nov 20-23. Though the designated 
high wind area may be overdone in terms of spatial coverage, the broadbrushed 
pattern aligns with the expected track of the mid-level trough, surface 
cyclone, and the associated cold front.



On Nov 23-24, colder air drawn in behind the storm system moving across the 
Central and Eastern CONUS may result in the first light freeze (32 deg F) of 
the season for northern and central sections of the Southern Plains. This is 
consistent with ECENS and GEFS temperature PET tools. According to the 
Midwestern Regional Climate Center, areas north of here have already 
experienced their first light freeze of the season. Therefore, a slight risk of 
much below normal temperatures is designated for the area denoted above from 
Nov 23-24.



California and southwestern Oregon may see a brief break in the active weather 
pattern early in the week-2 outlook period. After this, there is significant 
uncertainty as to how much Pacific moisture may reach this area. A subjective 
consensus of calibrated and uncalibrated ECENS and GEFS guidance warrants a 
slight risk of heavy precipitation for southwestern Oregon and much of 
California, Nov 22-26. A slight risk of heavy snow (6 inches or more) is also 
designated for the higher elevations of the Klamath and Sierra Nevada Mountains 
for the same period. Finally, a slight risk of high winds is posted for this 
same general area from Nov 23-26. Given the uncertainty involved, only slight 
risks were posted today along the West Coast.



Although the persistent longwave trough over the North Pacific is likely to 
result in periods of enhanced winds and precipitation to southwestern Alaska, 
hazardous thresholds are not expected to be reached.

FORECASTER: Anthony Artusa
